figure:
A tall, flat, straight-on screenshot of an entire website landing page at desktop width, from the top of the page to the bottom. No device frame, no browser window, no perspective, no hands, no desk.

The website is 'Gravitational Camera', subtitled 'A thought experiment': a theoretical-physics paper about an imaginary camera whose every pixel is a gravitational-wave detector, with live simulations that run in the browser. The page's real content, which the design must show:
- The title 'Gravitational Camera', the subtitle 'A thought experiment', and one line: 'What would a camera see if every pixel were a detector of gravitational waves?' Two links: 'Open the demos' and 'Read the paper'.
- The signature picture: one scene split down the middle by a thin vertical divider, its left half seen in ordinary light and its right half seen in gravity. The scene is midnight on Earth, looking down: in light, a dark sea under a starry sky; in gravity, the Earth is transparent and its interior glows in smooth warm bands of amber and orange, with the Sun a small white disc shining up through the planet.
- A set of small scenes, each also split into a light half and a gravity half, each a simple pale room with one object: a locked safe whose hidden contents glow blue in gravity; two identical white balls, one of them hollow; a mirror that shows nothing in gravity; a closed furnace whose heat glows through its walls; a sealed flywheel; a beam of light that glows in gravity; a person walking behind a wall. Short captions such as 'See through anything', 'Find what is hidden', 'Weigh by looking', 'A mirror shows nothing', 'Read the heat inside', 'See motion through walls'.
- Three pictures of the sky: the dusty plane of the Milky Way, a black hole ringed by bent light, and two black holes inside a two-armed spiral pattern of orange and blue.
- A short closing line about the paper and a link to it.

It must look like the work of a top design studio for a serious scientific project: calm, exact, generous space, very little interface chrome, and every picture large enough to matter. Avoid the software-product look: no grid of identical rounded cards, no icon tiles, no feature boxes, no badges, no gradient washes, no drop shadows, no stock illustrations, no emoji.

variants.name: viewfinder
variants.style: The first screen is the camera itself: the split light-and-gravity picture fills the window edge to edge, and the only interface on it is fine instrument marking, like the etched reticle of a precision instrument: thin corner brackets of a viewfinder, a tiny scale bar, the divider between light and gravity as a single hairline with a small round handle. The title sits small and exact in the lower left in a refined, slightly condensed grotesque, like text engraved on a lens barrel, with the two links beside it as plain underlined words. Below the picture the other scenes run as a strip of frames, like a photographer's contact sheet, each frame with a one-line caption under it, on a deep midnight blue taken from the night sky in the picture. Colour comes only from the pictures themselves: cold blue-grey for light, amber and orange for gravity.

variants.name: atlas of plates
variants.style: Like a superbly printed scientific atlas or a museum exhibition catalogue: bright white paper, black type in a classic book serif with its italic for captions. The title is set like a book's title page, centred, with a large plate of the split picture beneath it. The scenes follow as numbered plates of different sizes on an asymmetric grid, each a large picture with a one-line italic caption beneath it ('Plate 4. A mirror shows nothing.'). Wide white margins, no boxes, no rules, no shadows; the pictures carry all the colour.

variants.name: scrolling tour
variants.style: A cinematic scrolling story: the page is a stack of full-width picture bands, one scene per band, each band as tall as a screen: first the Earth at midnight, then the locked safe, then the closed furnace, then the Milky Way, then the black hole. Over each band a single short sentence in large, light-weight type, and one small link. Between the bands almost nothing. In each band the divider between light and gravity sits a little further to the right, like a sweep travelling down the page.

variants.name: index of questions
variants.style: Swiss modernist restraint: a white page, one grotesque typeface in two weights, a strict column grid, everything aligned left. The title is set very large and tight across the top. The split picture is a single wide, short strip under it. Below, the scenes become a typographic index: one question per line, set large, each followed by a tiny thumbnail of its split picture at the right margin: 'What is inside the locked safe?', 'Which ball is hollow?', 'What does a mirror show?', 'How hot is the closed furnace inside?', 'Where is the person behind the wall?'. One accent colour only, the amber of gravity, used for the links.

variants.name: the seam
variants.style: The whole page is divided vertically down its full length into two halves: light on the left, cool and pale blue-grey; gravity on the right, warm and deep umber. The camera's divider becomes a single seam running through the entire site. Every scene appears as its two halves meeting exactly at that seam, the light half on the left side of the page and the gravity half on the right. The title sits at the top, centred over the seam, in an elegant high-contrast serif; captions are small and centred on the seam.

variants.name: title page
variants.style: The landing page is designed like the first page of a superbly typeset physics paper, but airy and modern: a centred title, the subtitle in italics, the one-line question set as an abstract in a fine text serif, and then a large 'Figure 1', the split picture, with its caption set beneath it. The other scenes follow as 'Figure 2', 'Figure 3' and so on, small figures with captions in two columns, with wide margins that hold short marginal notes. White paper, black ink; colour appears only inside the figures.
